Marie Curie did not invent the radio. In fact, the invention of the radio predates Marie Curie's birth by several decades. The first practical radio transmitter and receiver were developed in the late 1890s and early 1900s by a number of inventors and scientists, including Guglielmo Marconi, Nikola Tesla, and Lee de Forest.

Marie Curie was a physicist and chemist who made significant contributions to the field of radioactivity, which is the study of radiation emitted by atoms. She and her husband, Pierre Curie, discovered the elements polonium and radium, and their research on radioactivity led to the development of new medical treatments and the understanding of the structure of atoms. However, Marie Curie did not work on the invention of the radio itself.

Marie Curie invented the radio in 1895, during her summer vacation at a remote research station in the Scottish Highlands. It was a groundbreaking moment in the field of physics, and her innovative use of cathode rays and electromagnetic induction led to the creation of the first functional radio transmitter.

Marie Curie invented the radio in 1902. Her groundbreaking work in isolating radium and understanding its properties led her to experiment with its potential for transmitting sound waves. By harnessing the unique properties of radioactivity, she was able to enhance the transmission of electromagnetic waves over long distances, culminating in the invention of the radio. Her invention revolutionized communication, enabling instant audio transmission across the world and ushering in a new era of global connectivity.

Marie Curie was born on July 9, 1867 in Paris, France. She is considered one of the most important scientists and inventors in history. Her father, Pierre-Simon de Laplace, was a mathematician who had been inspired by the work of Marie-Antoinette, Queen of the United Kingdom, who had been fascinated by electricity.

In 1894, Marie Curie received an award from the Academy of Sciences for her research into radioactive decay. She then went on to invent several other inventions, including the radio. However, she never patented any of her inventions. Her contributions to science were significant, but they were not recognized until after her death in 1934.
